source: Kaiser et al. (2025) CogniLoad
finding: A synthetic puzzle benchmark where intrinsic difficulty d (entities, attributes, rule clauses) is varied apart from length N and distractor ratio. Accuracy falls with d for all 22 reasoning models, but length N is the stronger stressor.
numbers: 22 models, 1,400 puzzles per config, d in {1,3,5,7,10}, N in {20,50,100,250}. By d=5, 12 of 22 models are below 50%. gpt-5 0.97 at d=3 and 0.82 at d=10; o3 0.93 and 0.80. Weakest models near 0.10-0.15 at d=10. Regression coefficient on d is negative and significant in every model.
limits: Synthetic logic puzzles; d is a bundle (state space, interactivity, clause count), not pure element interactivity. Max context 32K. Decline flattens beyond d=7 for most models. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Intrinsic complexity does cost accuracy in LLMs, but length of the chain costs more. S0 gate should count interacting items and also the number of steps.

source: Kaiser et al. (2025) CogniLoad: capacity points
finding: Fitted logistic model gives per-model ID50, the largest intrinsic difficulty each model holds at 50% accuracy. It ranges from negative (cannot reach 50% even at d=1) to about 19.
numbers: ID50: DS-R1-0528 19.07, gpt-5-mini 14.78, gemini-2.5-pro 12.74, gpt-5-nano 11.72, o4-mini 2.87, Qwen3-8B 1.0, Qwen3-32B -0.55, Phi-4-mini-reasoning -3.95. ECL50 above 300 only for gpt-5 and o3 class.
limits: Values come from a fitted GLM at mean N and distractor ratio; ID50 beyond the tested d up to 10 is extrapolated, not measured.
agent_relevance: A per-model capacity number can be measured. The decompose operator O3 should split until parts sit below the agent's own ID50, not a fixed number.

source: Kaiser et al. (2025) CogniLoad: distractors
finding: Extraneous load (distractor ratio) gives a U-shape: accuracy is lowest at intermediate needle-to-hay ratios and recovers at both extremes. Higher d deepens the dip.
numbers: Worst performance at needle ratio 25-50%. Recovery e.g. DS-Llama-70B 0.61 to 0.64, gpt-5-mini 0.84 to 0.86, gemini-2.5-flash-lite 0.38 to 0.53. Quadratic term significant in all but 5 models.
limits: Unexpected shape not explained by CLT; authors give no mechanism. Mean over models hides model-specific patterns.
agent_relevance: Mixed relevant and irrelevant context is the worst case. Cleaning context to nearly all relevant, or splitting off the noise, is safer than partly trimming it.

source: Wang et al. (2026) ToolLoad-Bench, cognitive load for tool agents
finding: Intrinsic load is defined as a weighted sum over edges of a tool-dependency graph (turn distance times 1+beta times same-type distractors). Accuracy falls with this load for every model, and an exponential decay fits well.
numbers: 500 tasks, 10 domains, 106 tools, 4.9 calls on average. Overall accuracy: xLAM2-32B 78.8, GPT-4o 68.0, Claude 3.7 Sonnet 64.8, Gemini 2.5 Pro 60.0, Qwen3-32B 55.2, Qwen3-8B 38.6, Llama3.3-70B 17. Fitted sensitivity k: xLAM2 0.034, GPT-4o 0.067, Qwen3-8B 0.085. Hosmer-Lemeshow p from 0.11 to 0.77, so no miscalibration found.
limits: Postulates (exponential success, independent nodes, additive load) are assumed, not tested against rivals. Only one benchmark family (built on BFCL v3 multi-turn). Fit quality shown by H-L test only.
agent_relevance: A countable proxy for element interactivity (dependency edges plus memory distance plus same-type distractors) predicts agent success. We can compute it in code before running.

source: Wang et al. (2026) ToolLoad-Bench: fine-tuning vs size
finding: A specialised fine-tuned 32B model resisted high intrinsic load better than larger general models. Low-load tasks were fine for most; Llama3.3-70B was weak even there (23%).
numbers: xLAM2-32B stayed above 60% in the high intrinsic load third; general models collapsed. Load buckets are thirds of the set.
limits: Buckets are thirds of one dataset; the cause of xLAM2's resilience is training on function calling, not shown to be load handling.
agent_relevance: Resilience to interacting elements can come from training on the task type, which echoes human schema effects. Scaffolds cannot replace that.

source: Shang et al. (2026) CoThinker, LLM coordination under CLT
finding: Splitting a high-intrinsic-load task across specialised agents helps on reasoning-heavy tasks and hurts on low-load instruction following. The boundary matches the CLT prediction.
numbers: LiveBench, Gemini models. One Math cell: 69.4 / 70.0 / 75.3 for MAD / DMAD / CoThinker. Instruction following: three Holm-significant losses for CoThinker. Agent count is non-monotonic. Several reasoning comparisons miss Holm correction at 0.05.
limits: The CLT link is an analogy; authors say proxies are design-time evidence, not proof. Gains over DMAD on Reasoning and Data Analysis not significant after Holm.
agent_relevance: Decompose only when interacting load is high. On low-load items one agent is better. This supports a gate at S0 rather than always splitting.

source: Shang et al. (2026) CoThinker pilot: attention entropy and instruction effects
finding: Proxy pilot: attention entropy rises with arithmetic difficulty. Longer instructions lower perplexity on hard tasks but raise it slightly on easy ones, a redundancy-like pattern.
numbers: Attention entropy 4.44, 4.80, 5.04 for difficulty levels 1-3. Perplexity on hard tasks 120.50 to 88.97 to 85.35 with richer instructions; on easy tasks 3.37, 3.42, 3.45.
limits: Three levels, one model family, no sample size or tests in the main text. Perplexity is not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Extra guidance is worth its tokens only when the task is hard. Skip scaffolding text on easy items.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Complexity of Theory-of-Mind tasks and Discrete World Models
finding: Complexity is counted as the number of state events needed to answer (necessary states, with spurious ones discounted), echoing Sweller. It correlates strongly with LLM error on five ToM benchmarks. Splitting the prompt by state events (DWM) helps on hard sets.
numbers: Models: GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4, LLaMA3-70B, Mixtral 8x7B. Hardest: FANToM, then ToMi, Adv-CSFB; easier: Mindgames, SocialIQa. DWM improved GPT-3.5 on Mindgames, FANToM, Adv-CSFB by a solid margin but was slightly worse on SocialIQa (short inputs).
limits: Correlation is across benchmark means, not a per-item test; no correlation coefficient in the text read. GPT-3.5 had memorised parts of ToMi.
agent_relevance: Splitting helps when there are many states to track and costs a little on short items. Another case for a gate based on a count.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: On puzzles with a complexity dial (disks, checkers, river crossing, blocks), accuracy falls to near zero beyond a model-specific complexity. Reasoning effort first rises, then falls near the collapse point. Three regimes: standard models win at low complexity, reasoning models win at medium, both fail at high.
numbers: Tower of Hanoi collapse at N=7-8 (100-200 moves) for reasoning models. Failure appears within the first 10-15% of the move list. River Crossing fails from N=3 (11 moves) while Hanoi N=5 (31 moves) is near perfect. At temperature 0, DeepSeek-R1 on Blocks World collapses at N=4; with sampling at N=30.
limits: Authors admit River Crossing N>=6 with boat k=3 is unsolvable and narrowed to N<6. Collapse point depends on the puzzle, not only step count. Claude 3.7, DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini family only.
agent_relevance: Complexity breaks the model in a regime pattern, so decomposing before the cliff matters. Do not add long reasoning on easy items (regime 1).

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking
finding: A comment argues much of the Hanoi collapse is output-length limits and unsolvable River Crossing cases, not reasoning failure. Asking for a generating function instead of a move list gives high accuracy in preliminary tests.
numbers: About 10 tokens per move; maximum solvable N about 12-13 for 64,000 to 100,000 tokens. Reported collapse before N=9 is below those limits, so models also stop early. River Crossing N>=6 with k=3 has no solution.
limits: Preliminary, no accuracy table in the text read; single author and the paper states Claude Opus co-wrote it. Shojaee et al. disputed it (failures begin in the first 10-15% of moves).
agent_relevance: Complexity limits depend on output format. Ask for a compact procedure plus code to run it, instead of a long enumerated trace.

source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic, the curse of complexity
finding: On logic grid puzzles with controlled search-space size and Z3 conflict count, accuracy drops sharply as size grows. Bigger models and more sampling help only at small sizes.
numbers: o1 81.0% overall, DeepSeek-R1 78.7%, o1-preview 71.4%, o1-mini 59.7%, Sonnet-3.5-1022 36.2%, Llama-3.1-405B 32.6%. o1-preview 17.0% on X-Large; others near zero. GPT-4o with oracle Best-of-N=128 reaches 69.1%, above o1-mini.
limits: The Best-of-N oracle uses the correct answer, so it is an upper bound, not a usable method. One task type, one-shot prompting.
agent_relevance: Search space size (not only count of items) is a usable difficulty measure. Selection with a real check is strong, which fits G3 and G5.

source: Dziri et al. (2023) Faith and Fate
finding: Tasks are cast as computation graphs, so depth and width measure complexity. Accuracy goes to near zero as graph size grows. Models seem to match sub-graphs seen in training. Single steps are usually right; composing many steps fails.
numbers: GPT-4 and ChatGPT reach about 59% and 55% on 3-digit by 3-digit multiplication. 82.3% of correct 4-digit by 2-digit answers had at least one error in the computation graph. Propagation errors exceeded local errors.
limits: 2023 models, before reasoning models. Theory part rests on assumptions about independent per-step errors. Training exposure estimated, not controlled.
agent_relevance: Per-step reliability is not the issue; composition is. Splitting into steps that code can verify matches G2 and O3.

source: de Jong (2010) CLT, educational research and instructional design
finding: A critical review. Intrinsic load is not only the count of interacting elements: content type, ontological category change and relation type add difficulty. The claim that intrinsic load cannot be changed by instruction is not held by all CLT authors. Total load is not clearly additive.
numbers: Klahr and Robinson (1981): a Tower of Hanoi variant (all pegs occupied) is harder with the same number of moves. Chi (1992, 2005) on category change. Simple-to-complex sequencing, part-whole and whole-part are described as ways to alter intrinsic load.
limits: Narrative review, no pooled effect sizes. 2010, before the 2011 Sweller book and 2023 definition.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a count alone. Our complexity measure must be checked against error per task family before it gates anything.

source: de Jong (2010): measurement and falsifiability
finding: Most studies use a single mental-effort rating, which cannot separate the three load types. Post hoc reading (germane if learners did well, extraneous if badly) lets nearly any result fit.
numbers: Wouters et al. found performance differences with no mental effort difference. Paas (1992) one-item scale is the dominant measure.
quote: every outcome fits within the theory post-hoc
limits: Opinion with examples, not a systematic search.
agent_relevance: Pre-register the prediction: which items should fail and why. Otherwise a load story can explain any result.

source: Klepsch, Schmitz, Seufert (2017) Two instruments for intrinsic, extraneous, germane load
finding: A short questionnaire with 2-3 items per load type. A three-factor model fits far better than one factor, so learners can separate intrinsic from extraneous load by self-report when items are phrased specifically.
numbers: Study 1 N=97; Study 2 N=65-95 per task. One-factor model CFI 0.612, RMSEA 0.071, AIC 2185; three-factor model CFI 0.970, TLI 0.951, RMSEA 0.021, AIC 845.
limits: Self-report; the germane scale is the weakest in later work. Learning-material samples, not problem solving.
agent_relevance: No direct use for an LLM. Shows load types can be separated at all, but only with explicit item wording.

source: Leppink et al. (2013) Instrument for measuring intrinsic, extraneous, germane load
finding: A ten-item scale; factor analysis found three components. Confirmed in three bachelor lectures and a randomised experiment.
numbers: PCA n=56 (PhD statistics lecture); CFA ns=171, 136, 148; randomised experiment n=58 freshmen.
limits: Only the abstract page was read. Later work questioned the germane subscale (secondary search result).
agent_relevance: Same as above: three types can be told apart by self-report in lectures.

source: Ayres, Lee, Paas, van Merrienboer (2021) Physiological measures of intrinsic load
finding: A review of 33 experiments (2016-2020) that varied task complexity within subjects. Almost all physiological measures detected the change, but sensitivity varied. Subjective ratings were the most sensitive. Eye measures led among physiological ones.
numbers: 33 experiments; most sensitive physiological measures: blink rate, heart rate, pupil dilation, alpha waves. Blood pressure and skin temperature failed but in only three studies. Memory and mental arithmetic tasks gave more sensitive results than simulations.
limits: Web of Science sample for 5 years; no pooled effect sizes. Short working-memory tasks differ from authentic tasks. Notes interactivity is not the only cause of load (recalling 12 numbers is harder than 5).
agent_relevance: Single-item difficulty ratings are a strong, cheap signal. For the agent: have it rate item difficulty, then check that rating against actual error.

source: Halford, Wilson, Phillips (1998) Relational complexity
finding: Capacity is better stated as the number of variables related in parallel (relational complexity) than as items held. About four chunks are processed in parallel, so quaternary relations are a soft limit. Higher relations are handled by chunking or serial processing.
numbers: Cites Sweller (1993) day-of-week problem as hard from interacting elements. Probe reaction time rises when the second premise is integrated (Maybery et al., 1986). Proportion a/b=c/d is a quaternary relation, hard for children.
limits: Manuscript version of the BBS paper. Four is a soft limit with a range. Arity is assigned by the analyst.
agent_relevance: Gives a way to count arity, not only items. Gate at S0: if a step relates more than about four variables at once, decompose first.

source: Krieglstein et al. (2025) Primacy effects in reporting cognitive load
finding: After learning units of low, medium and high complexity, the overall load rating follows the first unit seen, not the hardest or last. Self-report after learning is distorted by order.
numbers: Pre-study N=67; main study N=100. Regression on overall intrinsic rating: first unit beta=0.70 (95% CI 0.60-0.80), second 0.34, third 0.47. First-vs-overall distance smaller than last-vs-overall: 1.69 vs 2.47, t(52)=3.53, d=0.49 (increasing sequence). Interaction F(1,98)=19.01, partial eta2=0.16.
limits: Online learning videos on space topics; contradicts earlier problem-solving studies where the hardest task drove the rating. Rating, not performance.
agent_relevance: Order effects exist in self-judged difficulty. A model-written difficulty rating is also likely order sensitive, so use counted features (G5).

source: Krieglstein et al. (2025): prior knowledge and intrinsic load (citing Endres et al. 2023)
finding: The paper restates that element interactivity depends on both material and learner prior knowledge, and cites Endres et al. (2023): when task complexity is not obvious, higher prior knowledge can lead to higher intrinsic load in problem solving.
numbers: Secondary citation only; Endres et al. numbers not read.
limits: Secondary report of Endres et al.; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Expertise does not always lower load. An agent that knows a lot may still overcommit on a hidden-complex item. Detect complexity by count, not by feeling.

source: Chen, Paas, Sweller (2023) Defining and measuring task complexity through element interactivity
finding: Proposes that task complexity be defined by counting interacting elements together with the knowledge in long-term memory of the person. Structure is countable; learner knowledge is estimated by teacher judgment or tests.
numbers: Search summary only: a Year 7 study (N=156, Kadir et al.) found gains in achievement and self-concept after instruction that reduced element interactivity. No pooled effect size.
limits: Only search snippets seen; the publisher page redirected to login. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Confirms the count-plus-knowledge definition. For the agent the knowledge term must be estimated by testing it on sub-parts.

source: Chen, Kalyuga, Sweller (2017) Expertise reversal as a variant of element interactivity
finding: Argues the expertise reversal effect is the element interactivity effect seen through learner expertise: guidance that helps novices becomes redundant for experts because the same material has fewer interacting elements for them.
numbers: Not read. Claim only: both effects come from equivalent shifts in element interactivity.
limits: Only abstract-level text seen. The argument re-describes the effect and does not by itself discriminate CLT from rival accounts.
agent_relevance: Rival explanation to test: is reversal due to load, or to redundant text distracting attention? Same test applies to LLM scaffolds on easy items.

source: Tetzlaff, Simonsmeier, Peters, Brod (2025) Meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect
finding: A pooled analysis found high-support instruction helps low-prior-knowledge learners and hurts high-prior-knowledge learners.
numbers: About 60 studies, 176 effect sizes, nearly 6,000 participants. d=0.505 (low prior knowledge, high support better) and d=-0.428 (high prior knowledge, low support better). Figures come from a blog summary.
limits: Paper not opened (publisher redirect). Numbers are second-hand and need checking. No moderator details obtained.
agent_relevance: If correct, the reversal is medium sized in both directions: a scaffold can cost about as much for experts as it gives novices. Scaffold use should adapt to measured difficulty.

source: Ehrich et al. (2021) Item response modelling of cognitive load
finding: Relative difficulty (item difficulty minus person ability from item response modelling) can serve as a performance-based load index; working memory predicted it in numeracy and literacy.
numbers: Year 2 learners N=91; working memory significantly predicted the index in both domains (coefficients not read).
limits: Abstract and introduction only read. Children, standardised tests.
agent_relevance: A difficulty index from items solved versus model ability could replace asking the model how hard an item is. Links to item difficulty modelling.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking: effort versus complexity
finding: Reasoning models spend more thinking tokens as complexity rises, then spend fewer near the collapse point even with token budget left. The effect is strongest in o3-mini variants and weaker in Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking.
numbers: Five thinking models tested: o3-mini (medium and high), DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, Claude-3.7-Sonnet thinking. Pass@k comparison against non-thinking pairs at equal compute.
limits: Lawsen argues part of the drop is the model choosing to stop writing long lists; the authors reply that failures start early in the list.
agent_relevance: A model gives up effort exactly when load is highest. The program, not the model, should decide to decompose when a count says the item is above capacity (G1, S0).
